newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Car, sickness insurance growth areas in Portugal.
newsitem.headline: Car, sickness insurance growth areas in Portugal.

text.p: Motor vehicle and sickness and accident insurance will lead growth in Portuguese general insurance and consumers will buy such products mainly in banks and shopping centres, local brokers said on Wednesday.
"General insurance is growing mainly because of car insurance," said Jorge Henriques, managing director of Lisbon broker Sedgwick-Corretores de Seguros.

Jose Sanches, a partner with Credite-Corretores de Seguros, said car insurance had good growth potential because premiums were among the lowest in the European Union even though Portugal had the highest car accident rate in Europe.
He said claims had been higher than usual this year after one of the wettest winters this century.
Low car insurance premiums reflected Portugal's modest living standards within Europe, Sanches said. "Premiums should be proportionate to people's ability to pay," he said.

Fernando Aleluia, a director with Lisbon broker Joao Mata, said a recent European Union directive doubling the minimum civil liability required in third party car insurance to 120 million escudos ($777,000), had boosted premiums in Portugal.
Motor vehicle insurance rose 10 percent year-on-year to 153 billion escudos ($992 million) in the first eight months of 1996, according to the Portuguese Association of Insurers (APS).
Another promising growth area was accident and sickness insurance as people relied less on the indebted public health system, insurance brokers said.
Much of the demand came from companies offering disability income protection to employees as an alternative to the overburdened social security system, Sanches said.
Accident and sickness insurance grew 9.3 percent year-on-year to 78.6 billion escudos ($509 million) in the first eight months of 1996, the APS said.
APS president Ruy de Carvalho told Reuters last month that he expected accident and sickness premiums to grow by some 20 percent in Portugal this year, compared with 1995.
Increasing demand for sickness insurance resulted from disillusionment with long waiting periods and inadequate choice and facilities in state hospitals, he said.

Brokers said they expected insurance products to be sold mainly by retail and in-store banks in coming years, but they also saw good longer term prospects for telephone selling, now in its infancy in Portugal.

Portugal's two biggest retailers, Sonae Investimentos and Jeronimo Martins, have announced plans to open banks in their shopping centres in the coming months that will offer insurance and credit facilities.
"The big retailers will take advantage of the hundreds of thousands of people passing through shopping centres to sell them insurance," Sedgwick's Henriques said.

He said he doubted that big foreign insurers would muscle in on the Portuguese market as it was already overcrowded and the most attractive targets for acquisition were closely intertwined with Portuguese banks.
Some Portuguese insurers such as Mundial Confianca and Imperio own banks, while others such as Fidelidade belong to a bank.
Some 80 companies, many of which belong to Portuguese financial service groups or European insurers, now operate in Portugal, brokers said.
"There is a lowering of premiums in some areas such as industrial and fire insurance as there are many operators serving a small market," Henriques said.
($1=154.2 escudos)
